prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency standards with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a clean, original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping) with a decisive demonstration of its power (Ye's record systematic uncertainty and stability, near 1e-18). The result is a change of two orders of magnitude over the caesium standard, independently reproduced by several national and university laboratories, and it already drives tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second. The two-name credit maps cleanly onto the achievement. Having re-read the colleagues' arguments, B053 is the only shortlisted candidate that is supported by six of eight members in their top three, is mature, and has an attribution problem that is small compared with the others.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that optical clocks are a metrology achievement building on the frequency comb honoured in 2005 and on ion-clock work honoured in 2012, so some members may see it as incremental over earlier prizes or as an instrument rather than a discovery. Attribution to Katori and Ye also leaves out other lattice-clock groups (for example Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Takamoto) whose contributions were real. Against that, B013 and B033 are scientifically deeper in their field and B001 is the architecture of my own subject, so choosing B053 should not be read as a claim that precision measurement is more important.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first Sr demonstration plus Ye's push to 1e-18 are separable from the comb and ion-clock prizes, and agreement among clocks at that level shows maturity.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and maturity, and I think the separability argument is the right one: the comb and the ion clock were enabling or parallel steps, whereas the lattice scheme is what allows many atoms to be interrogated at once and that is where the stability gain comes from. Where I qualify his view is that the 'redefinition of the second' is a metrological milestone rather than a scientific one, and I would not let it carry the case. The case should rest on the fundamental-physics reach: gravitational redshift at millimetre scale and constraints on varying constants.

responses.point: Olsson placed B052 first, but about circuit QED (B001) she notes that it is adjacent to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits and that timing may be close, and that Girvin and Devoret are missing from the credited names.
responses.response: This is a fair point and it changes my own ordering. I ranked B001 first in my opening ballot, but I cannot be a neutral judge of it: it is my own field, and the 2025 prize was shared by researchers who visited my institution, which I flag below. Her adjacency argument is real even if I think the two topics are scientifically distinct, and the missing Girvin and Devoret credit makes a three-name B001 prize contestable. I therefore keep B001 as an alternative but do not lead with it. On B052, I accept that aberration-corrected electron microscopy is a substantial instrument advance, but I remain less persuaded it is a physics prize than the lattice clock, which tests physical law.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a durable organising principle, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the theory-plus-experiment core, and notes that the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions but not this discovery.
responses.response: I share his view of the scientific depth, and I ranked B013 second for that reason. My disagreement is about readiness of the prize, not merit: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal sits at the centre of the HgTe story and is not among the credited names, Hasan's three-dimensional work is a separate strand, and the three-person limit forces us to exclude people whose claim is comparable. A prize that cannot be allocated cleanly is weaker than one with a two-name credit. I would be willing to move to B013 if the committee settles that allocation, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs experimental discovery (B046) first as closing the Standard Model, and notes that the three-person rule strains a collaboration-scale result.
responses.response: The scientific importance is not in doubt and I do not equate his ranking with anything less than that. My difficulty is the one he states himself: choosing Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee over Della Negra is a compromise that rests on roles at the time of the announcement, which neither of us has verified, and it honours leadership of a collaboration rather than a discrete invention. I hold B046 below B053 on allocation, not on merit.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first with Halzen and Spiering, arguing that the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is secure and that source identification, though at modest significance, supports recognition now.
responses.response: I accept that the diffuse flux discovery is secure, but the individual source associations are at 3 to 5 sigma and the astrophysical interpretation is still moving, and I would prefer to wait for that. I also note that his own two-name configuration omits Karle, whom Danielsson includes, which shows that the attribution inside a very large collaboration is not settled either.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize.
Whether other lattice-clock contributors such as Lemonde or Ludlow would be seen as unfairly omitted from a two-name credit.
How much weight to give the circuit QED candidate (B001) given the 2025 prize, and whether the Girvin and Devoret credit gap can be resolved within three names.
I rely on recollection for clock uncertainty figures and priorities and have not verified them.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue on B001: circuit QED is my own research area (superconducting circuits, waveguide QED, microwave quantum optics), I lead the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, and my Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum work in the same field. Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I should not be the deciding voice on B001, and I have therefore not made it my preferred configuration. No specific connection to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile.
